utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam. Could I ask you, please, to read aloud the affirmation on the card that is offered to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell your name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: My name is Sarlota Fora.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And can you briefly outline your education.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I was born -- education, yes. I completed primary and secondary school and started studying at university in Belgrade and I graduated.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And where were you born and brought up?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I was born on the 4th of January, 1963, in Vukovar. And when I was about 1 year old, I moved with my parents to Belgrade. I went to primary school there and secondary school, and I studied there.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And when did you return to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I married in 1986 and I returned to Vukovar then.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how old were you during the events in Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: 28 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how well do you know the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I was born in Vukovar and that we had a family house there, I went to Vukovar very frequently with my parents and spent all my school holidays over there throughout my entire life. And also when I married, I lived there for a full five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: When you used to visit Vukovar and returned in 1986, what was the atmosphere like?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: In Vukovar the atmosphere was quite normal. I didn't notice any tensions or any inter-ethnic problems at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Did there come a time when tensions rose and was there a particular event in 1991 which led to this?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Tensions began to rise in 1990, towards the end of the year, and they culminated sometime in May 1991 when the well-known event occurred in Borovo Selo where the Croatian policemen were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what impact did this Borovo Selo incident have on the tensions in the area?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The tensions rose quite significantly. The topic was discussed a lot. The media had their part to play in the whole question of tensions. In the meantime, there were other events that took place, incidents, which contributed to raising the tension level. And I know of one particular event when another Croatian policeman was killed. That was sometime in June 1991, and so that's when tensions culminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, in 1991 which area in Vukovar were you living?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: My family house was at Mitnica and that's where I lived ever since I returned to Vukovar in 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And at the start of 1991 where were you working?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I was working in the utilities company which was also situated at Mitnica and that's where I worked as a secretary to all intents and purposes. I had to take care of some of our -- or rather, I monitored the work that was taking place at Novo Groblje, the new cemetery at Vukovar where there was a flower shop, there was mortuaries, and there was an office that the utility office had, its branch for funerals for those who had died or were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, did your job entail you leaving the office or were you remained in the office?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I would go to the new cemetery frequently on a regular basis. It was located at Mitnica, as I said, at the exit to town as you go towards Sotin.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you stopped going? If so, roughly when was that?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The last time I was at the new cemetery was at the end of August 1991, and as tensions had reached a peak -- or rather, not a peak but it was actually the start of the armed conflict, the conflict in that part of town. And it was very -- the situation was very difficult. I had to flee from the cemetery because a Yugoslav army tank passed through the wood between Mitnica and the new cemetery and blocked off that whole area. It shot at the cemetery, and at that point in time there about ten civilians at the cemetery. So after spending two hours in a small house at the cemetery taking refuge there and trying to hide, we decided to flee towards town.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I ask the court clerk to kindly display map number 6 for the witness, which is ERN 04626622 with exhibit number 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, shortly you'll see on the monitor in front of you a map. If you could just indicate to me when that's there. Witness, do you see the map? Has it come on the screen? Not yet.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the court clerk, would you kindly make some markings on that map with a pen. Now, can you please -- or can we zoom in a little bit, please, for the witness so -- onto the centre. A little bit more perhaps. Thank you. Now, Witness, you mentioned that you were living and working in an area known as Mitnica. Could you kindly circle the area on the map and mark it with an "A."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you used to travel to a cemetery to work. Could you kindly circle that area and mark it "B."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And can you please draw a line showing the route where you used to travel from your work in Mitnica to the cemetery and mark that "C."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you stated that you were unable to continue going to work due to the intervention of the JNA. Can you please mark on that map a line showing where these JNA tanks, I believe that you mentioned, came from, the direction the JNA came from.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The tanks cut across this area. It took -- they took the road through the woods. You can't see that here, so I'll draw it in roughly. And they positioned themselves opposite the cemetery. I don't know where they had come from, what direction, probably from Negoslavci or somewhere there, I can't really say. But they cut across the road near the first houses, and they reached the cemetery taking the road. And they positioned themselves opposite the cemetery. So they -- and they shot from there, targeting the cemetery and the suburbs of that area, Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, where you started to draw that line, could you just put a "D" there at the start.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, at this time where was your husband working?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: My husband, when we got married, worked in the post office, the head office, and he worked with the telephone installations and telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, can you please mark on the map the post office with a circle, if you can, roughly where it's located.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The post office was located at the mouth of the Vuka River into the Danube, so right by the banks of the Danube River, somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And could you please mark that with an "E."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, if we can keep the map on the screen with your markings, but we'll move away from that for the time being, what was your husband's job at the post office?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: At the post office my husband worked with a team of colleagues on the installation of telephone lines and installations and connections, which were linked to the switchboard at the post office. So that's the kind of work he did, telephone switchboard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, if you want this preserved, I suggest we should do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Well, I was hoping we could get to a few more questions for another marking and save it at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you think you will manage it in time. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I just hoped you hadn't overlooked it. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when Vukovar itself and Mitnica came under attack?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Mitnica was under attack from the beginning of the shelling of the town, and those beginnings were sometime in July. There was sporadic shootings which intensified, sporadic attacks, and towards the end of August the town was rocketed from planes. In September, there was intensive and ceaseless shelling of the town until Vukovar was occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And who was this attack by?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The town was attacked by the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, roughly how frequent was this shelling? Was it daily? Weekly? Monthly?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: During July it was sporadic; that is, shells would fall from time to time. And I remember attack on the so-called Becarski Kriz in Vukovar and the vinarija. That was in July. Then in August the situation was more or less the same, but the end of August is the event at Mitnica that took place, the one I talked about a moment ago. And towards the end of August there was also a rocket attack from the air where the workers' centre Vukovar was targeted. At the beginning of September, attacks became frequent and in fact there was 24-hour shelling, around-the-clock shelling of the town ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And now you've mentioned the round-the-clock frequency of the shelling. How intensive was it? Was it one bomb per day or -- roughly?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: When I say 24 hours of shelling, I mean continuous shelling of the town, that is to say, that the shells fell all the time and that the movement -- movements around town were very limited. You weren't able to leave the shelters at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And from your knowledge of Vukovar, were any normal buildings hit?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I was in a cellar myself and I would leave the shelter of the cellar whenever the shelling was less intense, whenever that was possible or, rather, when there was no shelling close to where we were where the explosion -- actually, explosions could be heard all over town all the time, but I would leave the shelter perhaps once a week and go to my house to see whether my parents were alive. And every time I ventured out of the cellar, what I saw in Mitnica was that, first of all, the roofs of the houses had been blown off, the roofs of the family houses. There were no other types of buildings there, they were all family houses with civilians living there. In the centre of town there were other more important buildings, if I can put it that way. But after that, the walls were destroyed, and at the beginning of November there was practically no house left standing above the cellar, above ground level. Everything had been razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, coming back to the months between June and August when you were working at the cemetery, did the number of people who were buried increase, decrease, remain the same?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: On several occasions, the number of people -- there were more people buried, larger numbers. During these sporadic attacks that I mentioned, they were very dangerous because this were sudden, unexpected, and a lot of people were killed during those attacks. And I remember one specific attack on the palace of Count Eltz, and to the best of my recollections about 12 civilians were killed there, persons who were living -- who were working in the palace, the employees of the palace. And actually, the palace housed a museum. The museum of the town of Vukovar was located in the palace building.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what was the status of those who were being buried at the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: What I have just mentioned is the employees of the palace, people who worked there, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, what had caused their deaths, so far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, the rocketing -- I'm not quite sure whether the palace was -- whether a rocket fell on the palace or a bomb that we called Krmaca or sow. But anyway, the palace was completely destroyed as a result of that attack -- or rather, part of the palace was razed to the ground. And underneath the rubble and ruins, the civilians that I mentioned who were killed were buried underneath the rubble.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that this shelling was intensive and frequent. So how were people able to carry out their everyday lives? Where did they live?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: We lived in shelters, in the basements of buildings, in cellars. And as we're dealing with Slavonija, I don't know how far you're acquainted with this, but that's an area where there was always a tradition of wine-making and there were lots of vineyards there. And all the households, generally speaking, had cellars for the wine. And so you could say that we had taken up residence in the cellars. We lived there for more than three months, day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how dangerous was it to move around outside on account of the shelling during this period, August to November 1991?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It was very dangerous to move around. You could only move around in a very restricted fashion, and any time you ventured outside of a shelter was risky business and you could lose your life. And I experienced that kind of situation on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how precise was the shelling?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, I can say that the shelling was very precise in that at a given point in time specific goals were targeted, were shelled, such as wells for water, that is to say, people -- that people used for their water supply. And I must say that Vukovar did not have any running water or electricity at that period, so people would go to the wells for their water. We had to make do as best we could. We went to the source. We went to houses that had a water source, that had wells. And the houses like that at Mitnica - and I saw three or four such houses - they were razed to the ground first.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, apart from the rockets which you mentioned, was there any other kinds of weaponry that was used?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes. All sorts of weapons were used. I can tell you the names for all those weapons. You learn fast. Even the small children who were in shelters learned to distinguish. This was raining down on us all the time. There were shells. There were projectiles from multi-barrel weapons. There were plane bombs. There were tank shells and missiles, which were the most dangerous kind of weapon being used, and these killed people even in the shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to a slightly different area, and this concerns the hospital at Vukovar. Now, between September and November 1991, how often did you travel from Mitnica to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Not often. As I've already said, movement was restricted about town. I only went once or twice under heavy artillery fire, so that later I gave it up altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And why did you go to the hospital on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I remember that once I went because I hadn't seen my husband in a long time, so we got in touch over telephone and agreed to meet up. I got a chance to go with one of the town's defenders who were driving the wounded to the Vukovar Hospital. I drove with him as far as the centre of town, upon which I walked back.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And did you reach the front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We reached the hospital, shells were falling all the time. It's very difficult to drive around in a car under such conditions since you can't hear a thing. Nobody much liked to drive around at the time, so that's why I decided to walk on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, if we can just go back to the map so we can make one final marking on this before we save it. And with the assistance of the court clerk, could you please draw on the map, when the pen comes, the route which you took roughly from Mitnica to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I took the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And if you could mark that with an "F," please.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: At the beginning, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, that will be fine. Now, as you travelled to the hospital along this route, what was the condition of the buildings like?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: As early as mid-September, most of the buildings had been damaged, roofless, walls torn down or damaged, pierced. You could no longer live in those buildings. They were no longer fit for habitation. There were no longer windows. The panes had been shattered, needless to say. But the trees were gone too. Or the road for that matter. The roads were no longer fit for travel. They were pot-holed. There were huge craters all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, can I kindly ask the Chamber that this map will now be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 119, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you reached the outside of the hospital. What was the condition of the hospital building that you saw?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The hospital building had been badly damaged. The windows shattered, the roof damaged. There were huge holes in the building, obviously caused by projectiles, drilling craters in the side of the building. I also noticed that the upper floors of the hospital were not being used at all, with the exception of the ground floor. There were no windows and there was no roof -- or rather, there was a roof, but it was severely damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, when you reached the hospital, how much heavy weaponry did you observe on the hospital which was capable of firing out?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I saw no weapons whatsoever inside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what markings, if any, did you see on the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The international hospital sign, the red cross, was visibly displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how big was the marking, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The signs were rather large and clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that after you were dropped off at the hospital you went to visit your husband at the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, if the court clerk could kindly show the last exhibit, I believe 119, just so the Court can see where the hospital is located in relation to the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, as you walked from the hospital to the post office, which I believe is marked "E," what were the state of the buildings like?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: All the buildings along the road were damaged, destroyed, roofless. The road was so damaged that it was very difficult both to drive and to walk. There was rubble strewn across the road, tree trunks lying across it, or there were no trees at all to be seen. And there was hardly anybody around. It was only natural that everyone was -- most of the people were in their shelters during the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And why didn't you drive? Would it have not been safer to drive from the hospital to the post office rather than walk?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: No, it would not have been safer. Quicker perhaps, but certainly not safer. The shelling was incessant, so we learned to listen carefully in order to know where a projectile was being fired from and how near it would be falling so that we could take shelter in good time from explosions. When you drive around in a car, you can't hear that sort of thing. You can't hear anything at all from all the din and noise, and that's why everybody preferred to walk instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what had caused all this destruction?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Ceaseless explosions, projectiles exploding all the time, all the weapons that I've mentioned. Bombs dropped by planes, heavy artillery, guns, tanks, multi-barrel rocket launchers. I was personally there when a plane that flew over the Danube at Mitnica, where our company used to be, it literally emerged from the river, flew low over Mitnica, gunning the neighbourhood with a heavy weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And who was it who was firing these rockets and projectiles and bombs, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you say that your husband was working in the post office I believe up to October and November. With all this shelling going own, how was he able to work in the post office?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: All the institutions that were still open at the time could not just proceed as usual. He did not work in the same place that he normally used to work at; he worked in an improvised office down in the cellar, much the same way that the hospital continued its work. The Vukovar auditor's office, whoever was still doing anything, going about their daily jobs in Vukovar, had to pursue whatever activities they had in cellars, in shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And roughly when did your husband cease working at the post office?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: My husband worked on until the 12th of November, which is when all communication broke down, all the telephone lines, the wireless lines that were still around. Everything was cut. The post office itself and the shelter were so severely damaged by this point that they could no longer be there, and most of the post office employees went back to their own homes, those who had survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned your husband worked there until the 12th of November. What did he do after that, until the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: He went back to Mitnica to our family home, and he was in the shelter with my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, did he join the defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: He joined the civil protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, if I can just come back to the period when your husband was working in the post office and you were living in Mitnica. How often did he come home each night?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: He didn't. He would only come back once a week or once a fortnight, depending on the intensity of the shelling. Whenever he could, in short. He would go to my company or, rather, our shelter and then we would go home together to check if our families were still alive. There were no communications, and after one whole day of shelling with so many projectiles being fired, somehow you tend to have this idea that perhaps no one but you made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So why didn't he come home each day?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I told you that movement was restricted and dangerous. You weren't free to just walk about town, and every time you ventured out, walked in the open from one location to another, usually ended badly. That was most usually the case. When we walked from my company's shelter to our home, it was very often the case that along the road we saw bodies of people who had been torn to shreds by shells with nobody there to remove their bodies and then give them a burial. Because nobody had noticed the bodies there, to begin with, with so few people passing by. It was a very common sight along that short trip from the centre of Mitnica to my home. I did see a great deal of this kind of thing since I had to go there every week.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to a different topic, and this relates to the Vukovar barracks. Now, were you aware that there was a JNA barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes. It was in a neighbourhood known as Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, when to your knowledge was this barracks blockaded?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't follow that specifically very closely. However, as we at Mitnica were being shelled ceaselessly, from the barracks and those general positions of the JNA until the very end. In addition to other positions that we were being shelled from, we were also being shelled from the Vukovar barracks, which means that they had a lot of ammunition and generally had a satisfactory level of supplies. It really didn't look as if they had been blockaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And this was throughout the period June until November?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes. Until Vukovar was occupied, Mitnica was being shelled continually from the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how precise was this shelling from the barracks into Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It was very precise. When I told you about the precise shelling of the water wells, then the Vukovar barracks is what I had in mind when I was talking about that, because that's where all the projectiles and missiles that were coming from that were hitting those specific targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, again I want to move to a slightly different topic, and this is concerning the company in whose cellars you were living during the conflict in the months of August to November 1991. Now, was this basement of the company also used as a ZNG headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The utilities company had very large cellars, old wine cellars dug deep into the ground and quite spacious. For this reason, after a while once all of their other facilities had been destroyed, the ZNG set up headquarters in our cellars, our company cellars.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, how often did you meet and mix with the ZNG officers in the cellar of your company? Was it daily? Weekly?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Once they had moved into our building, we spent the whole time with them. There were about 20 of us there at any point in time. We ate together. We were all together throughout. Those are people I know, people from Mitnica. The atmosphere was one of normal socialising and just getting on with our lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, while you were mixing with the Vukovar defenders in the basement, did you learn how much ammunition, food, equipment, et cetera, that they had?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: No. We knew about this because we were all in touch with our families back in our homes. Most of them were members of the civil protection. They stood guard. They guarded their own houses from JNA attacks and incursions. The ones that we were really scared of were the Territorial Defence members, their Territorial Defence. It was clear that our own defence, our soldiers, did not have sufficient ammunition, artillery, missiles, or even small rifle ammunition which was a staple in Vukovar at the time. When they came to the Mitnica headquarters, I remember that one of the town's defenders, a member of the ZNG, said that he had in his possession a missile that he had been keeping for five days now, waiting to receive more or other ammunition in addition to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, when you say "their TO," who do you mean by "their TO"?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I mean the paramilitaries, those people who were not members of the regular Yugoslav People's Army at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you seemed to mention that there's a distinction between the civil defence and the ZNG. What, if any, was that distinction? Can you explain.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The people's defence, what we call the people's defence -- or actually, this was in the early days of war, and Croatia had just come into existence, as it were. The ZNG were regular units established by the Croatian army, armed units. The civil protection or the people's protection were civilians were joined the town's defence, for the most part in their own areas where their family homes were. I would also include special services such as the fire brigade, medical staff, our utilities company. We all belonged to this thing called to the people's protection and we were all involved in the town's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you mention in your evidence that Vukovar seems to be being frequently and extensively shelled. What expectations, if any, did you have that the international community may intervene to stop this?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: From the early days of the clashes -- well, our lives were at stake, so of course we followed what was going on. We followed the media and the television. We followed the requests made by the Croatian government at the time that the international community should do something to protect civilians in Vukovar. We were hoping that in late 20th century Europe an entire town inhabited by 15.000 civilians would not be allowed to be destroyed like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how do you know the international community was even aware of your situation in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: There were comments being made by the UN, appeals were being sent out. We had our radios, we had our TVs. We knew what was going on around Vukovar, in Europe, or the world, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: In our estimate, roughly, at this time in October, November, how many shells were hitting Vukovar daily?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: As for the number of shells and missiles falling on Vukovar, I don't believe anyone ever really kept count. If anyone, the JNA should be in a position to know more about that, since they probably know how many missiles they fired on the town, how many missiles they used up. There were speculations in the media about this, that the number was 1.000, 1.500 a day, and so on and so forth. What I can tell you is this brief episode, where on one particular day we tried to count the incoming projectiles. We counted up to 100. This took about 15 or 20 minutes. The next time we did the same it took us about half an hour. So the intensity varied, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on to the period in time when it was decided that it wasn't really possible to hold out any longer against the JNA. Now, roughly on what date did it become apparent that the defenders could no longer hold out?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It was becoming more and more apparent as the month of November was drawing to a close. The destruction had reached such proportions that those projectiles who -- that did not explode against walls or roofs would fall down through into our shelters, resulting in more and more civilian casualties. There was no ammunition. There was no food. It was difficult to move about; ever since September it had been difficult. There was no help from outside; I mean the international community. Nothing significant happening to bring about a change in our situation. It had become clear that the town would have to surrender and that an occupation of Vukovar would ensue.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, when it was becoming apparent towards the end of November that the town would fall, why didn't any of the defenders try and break out and escape to Croatia in Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, at Mitnica - and I can speak about the part of town that I knew best - all the defenders there who were involved in the town's defence lived and had their families in that same area. That's where their family houses were, where their families lived, where their children and parents lived. And at the time, mostly of those people were living in shelters. So members of the Croatian National Guard and the armed members of the Vukovar defence -- it wasn't a professional army of course that had come in to fight against the JNA for the territory, they were all people who lived in the area, that's where their homes were, their families were. Of course they didn't want to flee and to breakthrough to another part and leave their nearest and dearest in a town under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So if the Vukovar defenders stayed because of their families, what options faced them? What choices did they have?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, a solution had to be found of some sort which would enable the civilians, first and foremost, to be in a place of safety. So people began to discuss what could be done and to discuss negotiations about the town's surrender or that part of the town's surrender. And the basic conditions laid down for that were that the civilians should be taken out to -- or evacuated to another part of Croatia that hadn't been engulfed by the war, and that the army hand over their weapons -- or rather, that the army should be treated like prisoners of war, pursuant to the application of the Geneva Conventions and war law.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So once you decided amongst yourselves that you would contact the JNA to negotiate a surrender, who on your side contacted the JNA to arrange surrender negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The members of the staff in command of the Croatian National Guards Corps and that part of town made a decision -- anyway, we had three negotiators, and they had contacted the Yugoslav People's Army via radio the day before and arranged to have negotiations held.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what were the names of your three negotiators, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Matija Mandic, Zdravko Komsic, and Filip Karaula. All of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And if you can -- please.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: All of them were neighbours, my neighbours, so I knew them all well. And we were there throughout those three months together.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, who did they speak to on the JNA side to arrange to meet to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I understood it that they would be meeting with the commanders of that part of the JNA, the commanding officers in Vukovar, stationed there at the time. As I understood it, the negotiations were to be held with high-ranking officers and I heard a name mentioned, Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, before it was agreed that the two parties would meet for negotiations about the surrender, was there any particular condition that was laid down before this face-to-face meeting could take place?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The conditions were the ones I mentioned early on, that is to say that all the fighters who surrender with their weapons should be listed in the presence of the International Red Cross and the observers, that they should be photographed, and that the Geneva Conventions should be applied to them, that they should be treated pursuant to them, and that they -- the people should be evacuated to a part of Croatia which had not been taken over by the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, why did the Vukovar defenders insist on a neutral party, such as the Red Cross, being present to broker the surrender negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, because they didn't think they could trust the JNA. It was clear at that time that they were cooperating with the Territorial Defence and in command of the Territorial Defence. So that is why the presence of a neutral party was sought to ensure that what was agreed was actually put into practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, your husband was working for the civil protection. What were your feelings as to what may happen to your husband if the Red Cross were not present when the surrender took place?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: What I thought would happen at the time, while in four months of the kind of life I had been living that I have described to you, is that if there were no international observers, if there were no neutral party, then not only my husband but nobody else, absolutely nobody else, would survive either, in view of the fact it was quite clear what their intentions were, that is to say, the shelling of town was so intense and there was such a lot of destruction, that that was the only goal. There could not have been any other goal but to destroy the town and everything in it, the civilians, the army, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, with the leave of the court I would like to put up a picture for you to look at, and it's a picture which has been taken from a video with 65 ter 311, V0000686, but has actually been now produced to bear ERN 04652854. So if the court clerk could kindly put up that picture bearing ERN 04652854. Now, Witness, can you tell me when you're able to see this picture.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the court clerk, if I may kindly ask you to circle some people in that picture. Can you circle in that picture the people who you recognise. Who, firstly, do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I recognise one of the negotiators, the man I already mentioned, Filip Karaula. Do you want me to put a circle around him now?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes. If you could put a circle around his head and mark that "A" just above, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I also recognise the other negotiator. He is turned -- he's got his back turned towards us, Zdravko Komsic, and he's sitting right next to Filip Karaula. But as I've seen a better photograph of these, I know that those are the two men I saw, Major Sljivancanin on that other picture as well, although you can't see him on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Well, keeping to this photograph, could you please circle and mark with "B" the other negotiator you can see and name him.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: That is Zdravko Komsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And you mention that you've seen another photograph or a continuation of this photograph with Major Sljivancanin in. Is there any part of Major Sljivancanin which is visible with this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I assume, in view of the fact that I have seen that other photograph, he was sitting at the head of the table. So I assume that the hands we see there are his hands, although I can't be quite certain. Of course, on the other photograph I saw, I saw Major Sljivancanin sitting at the head of the table and all the three Croatian negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, if you could just mark where those hands are which you believe are Major Sljivancanin and mark them with a "C."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And this gentleman to the left, which party is he from, do you know?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I think that that was Mr. Borsinger from the International Red Cross, who also attended the negotiations, at the request, of course, of the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Can you please circle him and mark a "D."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And is there anyone else in that picture you recognise from the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: No, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And before I ask the Chamber to exhibit this picture, if need be, would you be able to produce the other part of the picture which you say you have, showing Major Sljivancanin at the surrender negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I saw the picture after the exchange when I went to Zagreb and when I started working. Then I came into contact with one such paragraph, and I remember it very well, since it was something that I felt close to. I knew about the negotiations and I was, in a way, included. All of us who were at Mitnica were, in one way or another, included. So I did see the photograph. I think it is in the files of our office, but I can't quite be certain about that. I can, of course, find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, may I kindly request that this picture be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It had been received.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: In its blank format, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The original will be Exhibit 120; and the one that's annotated will be Exhibit 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, which date did the surrender negotiations take place in which these parties have met on the photograph you have seen?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It was the 18th of November, 1991. The negotiations were agreed upon the evening before, and the next day in the morning, our negotiators went to attend the negotiations, as had been agreed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, I'm wondering, Your Honours, whether this would be a good time to break so that we can pick up what was agreed at negotiations afterwards, or I can continue for the extra minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We judge from what you say, Mr. Agha, that this would be a practical and convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: It would be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because of a matter which must be dealt with by the Chamber during the break, we will have to have a longer break than usual. We will resume at a quarter past the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Judge Van den Wyngaert is unable to sit this afternoon. Pursuant to the Rule 15 bis, Judge Thelin and I consider the interests of justice will be served by continuing of the hearing. It will be necessary for Her Honour to view the tape and read the transcript of the proceedings this afternoon. It is certainly expected that she will be in a position to continue tomorrow. Yes, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, just to remind you before the break you mentioned in your evidence that the surrender negotiations took place on 18th of November and in the morning time. Now, what was decided in these negotiations in respect to civilians?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, we all waited with anticipation for the negotiations to end, and when our negotiators returned we were told that at the negotiations they had agreed that all the civilians from Mitnica should be evacuated to another part of Croatia which had not been engulfed by the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what did they tell you the negotiators had been agreed regarding the fighters who had been defending Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It was said that all the members of the Croatian National Guards Corps would surrender their weapons, that they would surrender, lay down their arms, and it was also agreed that they would be treated as prisoners of war with all the Geneva Conventions being applied and that a list of their names would be taken and that they would be photographed at the place of surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And where did the civilians and the defenders gather?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: About noon the negotiators returned and said that we had just one hour to comply with the evacuation and to go to a collection point which was a wide space on the way to the cemetery where the last houses were. There was a veterinary station there, actually. And the army was to arrive as well as the civilians for the evacuation to go ahead or the surrender to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Roughly how many civilians were there?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. I don't have any exact figures nor did anybody know exactly at the time, but I would say there were around 2 and 4.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And roughly how many defenders were there who were to surrender to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: There were about -- or rather, 150 to 200 defenders. I seem to recall a figure of 180, 180. It's difficult for me to remember all those facts and figures. I did my very best. I would say about 180, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what was the physical appearance of those who gathered there?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: After the intensity of the warfare and having lived in cellars for three months without any water or electricity and with barely any food towards the end, all the civilians looked in a sorry state. They looked very poorly. They were in a terrible state. They were all sad because after everything, they had to leave their own town.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, when you gathered, I believe you mentioned, at the veterinary clinic, where were you taken from there?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: That area was still under the control of our forces. We were all there, gathered there. The civilians formed a column and the army also formed its own column, together with the civilian -- apart from the civilians, that is to say the defenders of Vukovar, with their weapons. Two columns were formed. And during all these events there was radio communication between our negotiators and the JNA. Once everything was ready and put in place, one of the negotiators went in the opposite direction in a car, and when he returned he said that the evacuation could go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how did you travel to the place where you were to be evacuated from?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The columns of civilians and, parallel to that, the army column set out towards the demarcation line, separation line. And when the column passed through on foot, the people were walking, they were on foot. After them some 15 or 20 cars brought up the rear because some had set off in the evacuation in cars. So -- and at the end of the column there was a JNA armoured vehicle, and it accompanied the column to the new cemetery. My own family set out in one of those cars, whereas my husband and I walked to the cemetery in the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So when you got to the cemetery, where everyone who was surrendering had gathered for the evacuation, when was it that the fighters laid down their arms? Had they laid them down already or later?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The column of civilians and the column of fighters were going on foot side by side. The columns were stopped at the entrance to the new cemetery, in front of it, and that is where the handing over of the weapons took place. The Vukovar defenders handed over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, during the process of this surrender of weapons, were you aware of any international observers being present?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I did see an international observer, and I saw the president of the International Red Cross as well. I recognised the international observer by the white clothes he was wearing and the president of the International Red Cross because he had clear markings of the Red Cross on his arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: They were present during the surrender of weapons when the armed Croatian army laid down its arms, and they listed all the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that at the cemetery the civilians are in one column and the fighters in another column. How many JNA, roughly, were gathered at the cemetery to take the surrender?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, there might have been about 50 of them, as far as I was able to notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And who was in command of the JNA at the surrender?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Major -- the major of the Yugoslav People's Army, Sljivancanin, was in command. He was present there at the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: How do you know that he was in command?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, he was issuing orders, and it was obvious that his soldiers were obeying his orders. They collected up the weapons, they escorted the soldiers into the buses and trucks, and they addressed him in connection with the order given and the way in which it was to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Are you able to distinguish between regular JNA soldiers and paramilitary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia, all young men aged 18 to 26 had a military duty and they all had to go and do their military service. We all knew about the rules that prevailed in the army at the time. Members of the JNA all wore the same kind of uniform, olive-drab or camouflage. They had a five-pointed star on their helmet, while members of the Territorial Defence did not all wear the same kind of uniform. And they weren't as orderly as the JNA had to be. Some of the TO people sported beards and long hair, when it was a well-known fact that a member of the JNA could not wear a beard or long hair. They had to be clean-shaven with crew cuts.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, based on this distinction, how many paramilitary fighters did you see at the cemetery when the surrender was being taken?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I did not see any paramilitary fighters there. I only saw members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you mention earlier in your evidence that you saw international monitors and Red Cross being present. Was there also anyone else of particular prominence from the international community who you observed at the cemetery while the surrender was taking place?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: At some distance from all these events, there was a black car -- or rather, a dark car and several people wearing suits. They did not fit into the overall picture, so I had a closer look and I recognised Mr. Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what was Mr. Vance and his entourage doing?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: They were standing next to that long car watching the surrender of weapons and the incipient evacuation of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, according to your evidence it would seem that at the cemetery when the surrender took place there were civilians, some of whom came on foot, some of whom came on car, and also Vukovar defenders. Which group left the cemetery first or did all groups leave together?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The soldiers who had surrendered their weapons were the first to leave the cemetery. After that, the evacuation of civilians started, those who had arrived on foot. My husband and I walked all the way back to the rear of the column and joined my mother and father who were in a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what time roughly did you leave the cemetery, and did you go with your parents in your car or by foot?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: After I got into the car, we remained there for the next five hours, roughly speaking. All this was happening at about 2.00, before it got dark, which at that time of year is usually around 5.00. So I think the handover of weapons and the evacuation of civilians began at about 3.00 p.m. We remained sitting in the car until 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening with nothing much happening. It was quite obvious to us that the evacuation of civilians - and there were many of those - was taking some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And where had it been agreed that these civilians would be taken?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: One thing that was agreed explicitly during negotiations was that all civilians would be evacuated to Croatia, that is the part of Croatia that was not engulfed by war.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, when you left the cemetery, where were you initially taken?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: At about 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening we were told that we were to drive in a column and follow a military vehicle. We drove off in our cars following a military vehicle, and behind us there was another military vehicle. We were escorted all the way to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, as you travelled to Ovcara, what, if any, JNA weaponry did you observe?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: When you leave the main road leading from Vukovar to Sotin and turn into a local road to Ovcara, all along that road there were heavy weapons, heavy artillery of the JNA positioned. We saw it because we took that road and there were heavy weapons or artillery lining the road. The intervals between weapons were as little as two or three metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So how much weaponry was there, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say, but what I can say is that the road is perhaps two kilometres long or thereabouts and there was a weapon every two metres, virtually. Guns, multi-barrel rocket launchers, missiles. We were astonished at the amount of weapons there. We talked and we felt that it had been a miracle to even survive for that long inside Vukovar, given the amount of weapons that was being used against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you mention that you left the cemetery at about 9.00 or 10.00, so I'm assuming it would have been dark by that time. So how were you able to see all this weaponry on the roadside?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: All the cars had the headlights on. The lights were on, otherwise we would not have seen the road. There were about 20 cars with headlights on travelling down that road, plus the military vehicles. The weapons and the persons manning the weapons were standing by the roadside, just off the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And did you have a clear view of the weapons and those standing by?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes. We had a clear view. It was perhaps one metre off the road, not further.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And who were the soldiers who were operating the artillery, or at least standing by it?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Since we drew a lot of attention from the soldiers who were standing by the roadside near those weapons, they would walk up to the road and shout threats and insults at us. That is when I realised that there were both JNA soldiers and paramilitaries there.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what was the occupation of your father?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Up until 1999, more specifically May 1999 [as interpreted], my father lived in Belgrade. He was a member of the JNA, working there. He is a musician by profession, actually a music teacher. He is a violin teacher, and he worked with the military orchestra of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: What uniform did he wear, if any, while he was working in the JNA? Or was he in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: When they had rehearsals, the orchestra, they would wear civilian clothes. Whenever there was a celebration or ceremonies and concerts, whenever there was something official, he would normally wear a uniform to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how many years was your father in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: As a child back in Rijeka he went to the military school of music. He must have been 10 or 11 years old when he went sent to the army for the first time. He took classes there. He was trained to become a music teacher there, and he was later to become a music teacher at the military school housed in the Eltz palace in Vukovar. When I said that I'd moved when I was 11 years of age, that was because the entire military music school was moved to Zemun with all its pupils and teaching staff. My father had to move to Belgrade. He was transferred to Belgrade, so the family had to follow suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So how familiar are you with the JNA uniform would you say?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: My father always had a regular uniform for the everyday purposes and one for festive occasions, for more formal occasions, which he sometimes needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how familiar are you with the appearance and tidiness and turnout of JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I was quite familiar with that. I had a very good idea what a soldier was supposed to look like, a JNA soldier, clean-shaven, clean, cropped hair, and neat uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: My apologies. I think there's an error on the transcript. I think at 15 -- 16.40.54 it should read May 1989 rather than 1999 -- if I might clarify that with the witness. I apologise. It's disappeared from my screen. But when was it that your father left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: My father was supposed to retire in September 1991. There was an unwritten rule in the army that three months before an officer retired, the officer was no longer supposed to report to work. They had no obligation to be physically present. So he stopped going to work three months before the official date of his retirement. That was customary in the JNA at the time. So as soon as he could afford to stop going to work, he went back to Vukovar with my mother, moved back to our family home, and this was in May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you clarified your ability to distinguish between JNA and non-JNA, and I want to come back to the part where the surrender took place at the cemetery. And with the leave of the Court, if we could kindly show Exhibit 59 again, and I would request the witness to make some markings on that so that the Court can be familiar with the area she's talking about. If the court clerk could kindly help her with a pen or Magic Marker. Now, Witness, when the map appears on your screen you can let me know, but it will be the same map we were looking at last time except this time I would ask you to make different markings on it and mark them "A," "B," and "C" accordingly. So if you will let me know when the map has reached you.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: No map yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Not for me either.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I have it now. The map has appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Is it possible we could zoom in one time, please. Oh, no, no, no, back, back, back. Once more forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you please, once again, on this map draw a circle where Mitnica is and mark it "A."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Can you then, please, mark, if you're able, the area roughly where you gathered in the veterinary clinic before moving to the cemetery and mark that "B."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And could you then please mark the cemetery where the area was where all the surrendering people had to gather and mark that "C."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And can you please then draw a straight line, if you're able, or a line showing the route from which you got from the veterinary clinic marked "B" to the cemetery at "C."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could just put a "D" there somewhere or other along the line.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can you please circle where Ovcara is and mark that with a "D."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And can you draw in red the route which you took from the cemetery to Ovcara -- I'm sorry. It seems to be two Ds. Perhaps we could make that an "E," that last one.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And if you would kindly draw the route which you took from the cemetery to Ovcara just by way of a line.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And then maybe mark that line with an "F."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And can you please now mark on that map the area where you say all the artillery was placed which you observed en route to Ovcara with "Xs."

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I ask that this map with the markings be exhibited, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 122.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all with the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, what time roughly did you reach Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It doesn't take long to get from the cemetery to Ovcara. It takes about 20 minutes. I think we reached Ovcara at about 10.00, 10.00, half past 10.00, depending on when exactly we'd set out. I can't be more specific about the time. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, how many civilians were there in your convoy, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: There were about 20 cars. All the cars were full, which means there were four or five persons in each one, which leads me to conclude that there were about 100 or perhaps 120 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what were the composition of these people? Were they men, women, children, or just women?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: There were men, there were women, women with children, and elderly, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: What arms did any of these people have with them?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: No arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what happened when you reached Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Once we were there we were instructed to park at the plateau, the open area, near the hangar there. It was unlit. We were instructed to leave our cars and leave the car keys on the front seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, roughly how many JNA soldiers did you observe at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I observed both JNA soldiers and TO or paramilitary members, if you like. That was on the way there. Once we reached our destination, there was no lighting and I only saw those who were standing in that open area. I did not see any of those who were standing nearby in the dark. In terms of those whom I'd seen along the roadside, I reckon I'd probably saw more than a hundred of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: When you say "those," are you referring to JNA or JNA and paramilitaries or both?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Both. They were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, coming to Ovcara itself, did you again see both JNA and paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes. I saw JNA members. I saw Major Sljivancanin, who introduced himself. He was accompanied by two paramilitaries. They were obviously paramilitaries because they both sported long hair and a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And who was in charge of the JNA and paramilitaries at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It was quite clear that a JNA officer was in charge or, rather, giving orders, specifically Major Sljivancanin. He was the one who addressed us. He introduced himself, and he gave a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what did he say, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I will try to re-interpret the essential part. At the outset he said that we, the citizens of Vukovar, should know exactly why we were now there in that place. He said that they had liberated Vukovar and that we were those who had been killing his young boys.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: How did you feel? Did you feel liberated?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Not at any point in time did I feel a need to be liberated or set free during the war in Vukovar. I was living in my own town, in my own house. I had no need for anyone to come along and set me free.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, the people who were with you at Ovcara were from Mitnica. What, roughly, in percentage terms was the ethnic composition of Mitnica during the battle?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Generally speaking, one thing that one must keep in mind is that Mitnica was a part of Vukovar that had a 99 per cent Croat population. That part of Vukovar was, for the most part, inhabited by ethnic Croats. As a result, most of those evacuated from Mitnica were also Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how heavy had the fighting been around Mitnica between the Vukovar defenders and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: I still remember several cases when the JNA stopped shelling and tried to breakthrough the lines using their infantry. I remember that our soldiers displayed exemplary bravery on those occasions, managing to repel a far superior enemy. I remember, based on the accounts of Vukovar defenders, that the JNA suffered a significant number of casualties on those occasions. So did the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, coming to Mr. Sljivancanin's -- or sorry, Major Sljivancanin's speech at Ovcara, returning to that, presumably it was quite dark by now, so how were you able to see Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: It wasn't a large group of people. There were about a hundred of us - I really don't know the exact number - and we were all standing on a little plateau. And not far from us, just a few metres from us, was Major Sljivancanin and the two members of the paramilitaries I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned that there were elderly women and children within your group. What happened to this part of your group?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin at the end concluded, after a lengthy speech, by saying that the evacuation would take place of all of us as had been agreed at the negotiations, and that the people to start out first would be the elderly and women with children. So they were set aside first and boarded the buses first and were driven off.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And where were they meant to be taken? Can you please remind the Court, according to Mr. Sljivancanin and the surrender negotiations.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Both on the basis of the conclusions of the negotiations and on the basis of the speech delivered by Major Sljivancanin, these people were supposed to be taken to a part of Croatia which was not in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And where were they, in fact, taken?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: A portion of them were obviously taken to Croatia, whereas another part were taken to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: How do you know that another part were taken to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Because I saw them there. Since I myself, after the evacuation to the free part of Croatia, ended up in the Sremska Mitrovica prison, and Sremska Mitrovica is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, after the elderly, women, and children had left, what was said regarding the remainder of the people?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin said that the men had to be separated from the women next and that we were all going in the same direction, but that it was necessary for us to be separated. And the women refused and they remained standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So after the men and women refused to be separated, how did Major Sljivancanin react? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: After that, there was a lot of discussion. They stood aside from us, civilians, standing there, and quite obviously there was a heated discussion between Major Sljivancanin and members of the paramilitary formations. I think there was some members of the regular army there, too, the JNA. They had this discussion and debate, and after that Major Sljivancanin left the group, came back to our group, and said that we should all board the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And where were you meant to be going?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: According to what was said, we were supposed to go to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, as you were boarding the buses at Ovcara to leave, did a paramilitary soldier say anything to your husband?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The members of the paramilitary units or the two members mentioned that were standing together with Major Sljivancanin at Ovcara while he was delivering his speech were standing at the entrance to the buses which we were supposed to board. And while we were getting on and passing by them, one of them, the one standing at the entrance where we were boarding, he addressed -- he spoke to my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what did he say to your husband?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, when we got into the bus I asked him what the soldier had said to him, and he said that he had recognised him when he spoke and when he saw him close up, because he went right past him, right next to him. He recognised him as a man called Pero, his nickname was Limun, or Lemon, who worked at in Mitnica in a shop there, and who said that they had to release us now but that it was to have finished differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: In your view, what did you take this to mean?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Well, I think the comment can be understood in only one way. If they were indeed releasing us and matters would have ended differently, that means that they were not supposed to release us but that we were supposed to remain at Ovcara. And if we were evacuated alive, if we survived, then if things should have ended differently it would mean that we should not have been left alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier that there was heavy fighting in the Mitnica area and the JNA suffered heavy casualties and indeed both sides. So what was the attitude of the paramilitaries at Ovcara towards you?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Very hostile. While the column of cars was passing by, they shouted out to us, they issued threats, they swore. And while we were getting on the bus, they were quite obviously hostile in their behaviour; they were extremely angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, according to your evidence you were meant to be taken to part of Croatia where there was no fighting. Where, in fact, were you taken to from Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: At around 2.00 a.m. or, rather, early the next morning we reached the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. That is a prison which is located in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, who was escorting you there?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: We were in the buses, and also in the buses were armed members of the Yugoslav People's Army and the driver who was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, as you travelled from Ovcara to Sremska Mitrovica, do you remember any of the areas you passed through at all?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: We went via Negoslavci and Oriolik, I remember that, and then we reached the highway, where we stopped and where we were forcibly separated into different buses, the men separated from the women.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And where did the separate buses proceed? Did they proceed to the same place or a different place?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: The same place. So I wasn't quite clear about the logics of that separation, why we were separated the men from the women, whereas they actually sent us to the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, turning back to the villages you passed through like Negoslavci, were these villages primarily of Serbian ethnicity or Croatian? What was their majority make-up?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Negoslavci is a village inhabited predominantly by Serbs, and along the way we would comment and say that those places were absolutely left intact. They were not damaged in any way. The houses were standing quite normally as if there was no war going on in those parts, whereas its just a few kilometres away from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you say you ended up in Sremska Mitrovica, in Serbia. What kind of place was this where you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Sremska Mitrovica is a prison, which in the former Yugoslavia, criminals, killers, served their sentences, all those convicted of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance of the court clerk and the leave of the Court, I'd like to show Exhibit 103, which is map bearing ERN 0462-6620.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: When you see this map on the screen, Witness, if you could let me know, and I will ask you again to make some markings on it for the benefit of the Court.

utterances.speaker: SARLOTA FORO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the map.
